title: 3-Read Friday #29: Worked Examples, Pupil Premium and SEND, and Khanmigo
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 29 gathers three posts that each push back on an assumption Barton holds. His first pick, Dylan Kane's "How I Use Worked Examples," is framed as a direct challenge to Barton's own well-known preference for live-modelled worked examples, noting that Kane - like Michael Pershan - instead has students study already-completed examples, a genuinely different approach Barton flags as worth serious thought. His second selection, Marc Rowland's piece on Pupil Premium and SEND, prompts an unusually candid admission that Barton doesn't think enough about supporting SEND students, and he singles out Rowland's line "the practitioner is the intervention" as the single most powerful takeaway. His third pick, Dan Meyer's "Khanmigo Doesn't Love Kids," is introduced as a useful corrective to AI-tutor enthusiasm, with Barton noting that even as large language models demonstrate genuinely impressive capability, it's worth pausing to examine their current limitations rather than assuming transformation is imminent. Across all three picks, Barton positions himself less as a neutral curator and more as someone actively updating his own views on worked examples, SEND support, and AI in the classroom.
points: Barton frames Dylan Kane's worked-examples piece as a genuine challenge to his own established practice, contrasting Kane's study-a-completed-example approach with his own preferred live-modelling method.

His response to Marc Rowland's Pupil Premium/SEND piece is unusually self-critical, admitting he doesn't think anywhere near enough about supporting SEND students, and singles out "the practitioner is the intervention" as his key takeaway.

Barton positions Dan Meyer's Khanmigo critique as a useful counterweight to AI-tutor hype, framing it as worth pausing to reflect upon their current limitations even amid genuinely impressive large-language-model capability.
The issue pairs two pieces that directly challenge Barton's own prior assumptions with one that tempers his general AI enthusiasm, giving the issue a self-correcting editorial tone.
quotes: Regular readers may know just how obsessed I am with worked examples.
Like Michael Pershan, Dylan favours students studying completed worked examples instead of watching the example being modelled live by the teacher.
I don’t think anywhere near enough about supporting SEND students. This post by Marc has helped educate me.
The practitioner is the intervention” is one takeaway I found particularly powerful.
Amercian educationalist, Dan Meyer, is not a fan of AI tutors. Here, he shares an exchange with one of the most prominent of these, Khanmigo from Khan Academy.
With the incredible things that large language models like Chat GTP can do, it is interesting to pause and reflect upon their current limitations.
